reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it presents a Forsage invitation that promotes high earnings in exchange for funding a mobile wallet and paying 10 BUSD to register and activate slots. It promotes referral-based rewards, reinvestment, paid upgrades, and purchasing multiple slots as ways to increase income, directly soliciting paid participation in the crypto slot structure. the available video evidence does not claim that actual payments, withdrawals, or participant losses were proven.

opening.argument: The presentation emphasizes a rules-based system rather than discretionary promises: it describes Forsage as having “zero human factors” and says its policy cannot be changed because it operates on blockchain. Its stated case is that participants can inspect activity and payouts, not that a speaker can alter accounts or conceal a central operator. The slides also distinguish possible lost profit from extra profit, acknowledging that a participant can miss an upgrade and lose a payment opportunity. That is a material risk, not an assurance that every viewer will earn. These points do not prove the system is safe, but they support reading this as an explanation of a risky automated program rather than a demonstrated deception.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution treats wallet funding and slot payments as proof of deceptive solicitation, but payment is not itself proof of deception. The cited referral passage explains who receives a payout in an example; it does not establish that payments were fabricated, withdrawals blocked, or losses concealed. The record expressly leaves actual payments and participant losses unproven. That gap matters when distinguishing an openly described, risky program from a proven scam.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling the system automated and transparent does not answer the central concern: the presentation asks viewers to fund participation and describes returns tied to recruiting people into positions. It even says the first five X3 levels total 155 BUSD and explains that higher slots affect access to further income. A warning about missed upgrades is not a general risk disclosure, and claims of visible activity do not establish that participants can recover their money or that recruitment-based payouts are sustainable.

opening.argument: This is substantially a walkthrough of how a blockchain-based program is presented to work. The speaker defines centralized versus decentralized systems, explains wallet options, identifies BUSD, and proceeds through X3 and X4 slot diagrams and their recycling rules. The material is not a report of verified participant outcomes: it lays out the program's own mechanics for viewers to understand. The title itself identifies it as a presentation, and the slides function as a stepwise visual demonstration. The invitation and promotional claims are present, but they do not erase the explanatory character of the bulk of the material or establish that the mechanics described were fraudulent.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution's selected lines are instructions within the walkthrough, but they do not establish that the video proves payments or losses. Its own opening concedes that outcomes were not proven. Explaining how registration, referral positions, and recycling are said to work can be instructional content about a program, even when the speaker promotes it. The record does not show a concealed mechanism or false transaction evidence; it shows a presentation describing the mechanics and soliciting interest.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A tutorial can still function as a solicitation when it walks viewers through creating a wallet, funding registration, choosing paid slots, and recruiting participants for income. Here the speaker does not merely explain blockchain concepts: the presentation calls the plan “100% working” and tells viewers how to join and increase their slot position. Calling it a demonstration does not change the recruitment-based payment structure it teaches.

opening.argument: The presentation describes a paid digital program with stated slot prices and a wallet-based registration process. A fee and a purchase structure alone do not establish a scam; the relevant question is whether the record shows deception, stolen credentials, or an actual failure to deliver. It does not show a request for passwords: the speaker says the program has no password, and the registration explanation names wallet software and transaction fees. The slides also frame the amounts as BUSD slots rather than disguising the payment as an unrelated charge. While the video makes promotional earning claims and discusses recruitment, these materials do not independently establish that a promised payout was withheld or that anyone suffered a loss.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution points to the entry amount and referral payouts, but neither fact alone proves a fraudulent transaction. The available evidence does not show passwords being solicited, funds disappearing, or promised withdrawals failing. Nor does a diagram of positions establish that any actual participant was paid or harmed. The case for calling this ordinary paid participation is limited, but it is at least consistent with the explicit, itemized slot and fee descriptions in the presentation.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The program is not presented as an ordinary product with an independent benefit delivered for the price. The speaker links income to bringing people into the team, describes payouts by their position, and says later income requires upgrading to more expensive slots. Those are the defining features of the promoted mechanism, even without proof of actual losses or credential theft. A disclosed price does not make recruitment-based earnings ordinary commerce.
